content: The trans effect in inorganic chemistry refers to the phenomenon where certain ligands, known as trans-directing ligands, weaken or destabilize the bond of another ligand located trans to them. This effect is primarily attributed to electronic interactions and is most prominently observed in square planar complexes, although it can also occur in octahedral complexes. Beyond its kinetic implications, the trans effect also influences the ground state properties of a molecule, such as bond lengths and overall stability. Some researchers distinguish between the kinetic trans effect and the structural or thermodynamic trans effect, using terms like trans influence to describe the latter. The trans effect was first identified and named by Ilya Ilich Chernyaev in 1926. Kinetic Trans Effect The kinetic trans effect is characterized by the increased rate of substitution of a ligand located trans to a trans-directing ligand. The strength of the trans effect follows a specific sequence, with ligands like fluoride (F−), water (H2O), and hydroxide (OH−) exhibiting weaker trans effects, while ligands such as hydride (H−), carbon monoxide (CO), and ethylene (C2H4) exhibit stronger trans effects. A classic example of the kinetic trans effect is the synthesis of cisplatin. When starting with the PtCl4²⁻ complex, the first ammonia (NH3) ligand can bind to any of the four equivalent positions. However, the second NH3 ligand preferentially binds cis to the first one because chloride (Cl−) has a stronger trans effect than NH3. Conversely, if the starting complex is Pt(NH3)4²⁺, the product formed is trans. The kinetic trans effect in square planar complexes can be explained by an addition-elimination mechanism involving a trigonal bipyramidal intermediate. Ligands with a strong trans effect, such as phosphines (PR3) or hydride (H−), tend to occupy equatorial positions in this intermediate due to their high π-acidity or low lone pair–dπ repulsion. The incoming ligand also occupies an equatorial position, and by the principle of microscopic reversibility, the departing ligand must leave from an equatorial site. The trans ligand occupies the remaining equatorial position, leading to the formation of the kinetically favored product where the ligand trans to the one with the strongest trans effect is eliminated. Structural Trans Effect The structural trans effect can be experimentally observed using X-ray crystallography. It manifests as an elongation of the bond between the metal center and the ligand located trans to a trans-influencing ligand. For example, strong trans-influencing ligands like hydride can cause bond elongation of up to 0.2 Å. A smaller cis influence can also be observed, but it is generally less pronounced than the trans influence. The relative magnitudes of the cis and trans influences depend on the formal electron configuration of the metal center. Theoretical explanations for these effects often involve the specific atomic orbitals participating in bonding.
